description:
Hi, I'm Ofori, a KNUST CompE undergrad & ACES Coding Club Pres blending AI/dev (Angular/ML) with pro motion graphics. For Challenge 09 ("Abandoned but not Forgotten"), I'm building an interactive, gamified web museum of NASA's discarded lunar/Martian hardware. I'm handling frontend, AI, and video.

I need:

Space History Researcher

UI/UX, Pixel, or 3D Artist

Backend Developer

Let's build the greatest outdoor museum in the universe. Reach out!
summary: Ask the Machines brings 12 machines NASA left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space back to life for ages 9–14. Visitors travel through three worlds, follow a trail of machines and read or listen to each one’s first-person story, with an illustration, a short mission video, its status today (silent, still talking or grounded) and a fact check. A 3D Mission Lab lets users rotate spacecraft models, and an AI astronaut guide answers questions from our story notes. It turns forgotten hardware into stories that make space history memorable and accessible.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Ask the Machines is an interactive website that brings 12 real machines NASA left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space back to life for ages 9-14 and casual space fans. Visitors start at a 3D carousel of three worlds (the Moon, Mars and the outer solar system), then follow a curvy trail with one stop per machine: Surveyor 3, the Apollo 11 Eagle descent stage and laser mirror, the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicles and the Apollo 17 science station on the Moon; Sojourner, Opportunity, InSight and Ingenuity on Mars; and Pioneer 10, Voyager 1, Voyager 2 and New Horizons in deep space. [Each world ends with a mini-game.]

Each machine has its own story page. The story is told in the machine's own voice and follows the same arc: who I am, how I worked, what I found and where I am now. Every page has a flat 2D illustration, a status badge (silent on the surface, still talking, grounded and so on), a short mission video, a "Fact check" section with sources and a "Listen" button that reads the story aloud. The site picks the best available voice automatically, and visitors can choose their own and change the speed. A Mission Lab lets visitors rotate, zoom and explore 3D models of an Apollo lunar module, a Mars rover, Ingenuity and a Voyager probe. An AI astronaut guide named Apollo answers questions using only our own story notes, and says "I don't know" when the notes don't cover something.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Young people mostly hear about active missions. This project shows that the machines left behind did real science that made later missions possible: Surveyor 3 showed the Moon's ground could hold a lander, Apollo's mirrors still measure the Moon's distance, InSight listened to the inside of Mars, Voyager entered interstellar space. We want visitors to feel a personal connection to these silent explorers and to see how each discovery led to the next mission. Audio narration, plain language, keyboard navigation, reduced-motion support and a phone-friendly layout let more people learn from it, including younger readers and people who prefer to listen.

HOW NASA AND SPACE-AGENCY INFORMATION MAKES IT POSSIBLE

The stories are based on public NASA and JPL mission information and archives, and each story includes a short mission video from NASA, JPL and other public sources. The real science told through the stories includes the Apollo laser reflector, InSight's marsquake recordings, Voyager's journey into interstellar space and Ingenuity's first powered flight on another planet. For Voyager's live distance we point visitors to NASA's own mission status page instead of hard-coding a number.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

Angular with server-side rendering; TypeScript, HTML and CSS; Three.js for the 3D world carousel and the Mission Lab model viewer (glTF/GLB models with Draco compression); a Node/Express server; the browser's Web Speech API for narration; and an NVIDIA Nemotron language model, accessed through NVIDIA's API, behind the Apollo guide, grounded in our story notes with a fallback when the service is unavailable. Videos are embedded through YouTube's privacy-enhanced mode. We built it on laptops using VS Code and Git/GitHub. AI tools helped us build it: we used OpenAI Codex to help write code, Google Gemini to help create the machine illustrations and presentation, and Claude to help draft story copy and prompts. We reviewed and edited the outputs ourselves. 3D models are credited on the site: Mars rover by Rasmus.Eist, Ingenuity by Marco_Romero and Sakado, and the galaxy model by 991519166 (all CC BY 4.0, via Sketchfab).

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Instead of a fact list, each machine speaks for itself, with its own personality: a cautious scout, a stubborn rover, a quiet listener, a tiny helicopter. Visitors travel between worlds in 3D, hear the stories read aloud, hold the spacecraft in their hands in 3D and ask a friendly astronaut guide questions. The design is one consistent look across the site: a dark space background, gold accents and a white astronaut mascot.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Accuracy: every story has a Fact check, and creative lines are labeled. For example, Opportunity's famous "my battery is low and it's getting dark" was a poetic reading of its final data, not a literal message, and we say so. The AI guide may only answer from our reviewed notes. Audience: simple language and short sections for ages 9-14, no accounts or personal data collected. Accessibility: keyboard use, audio narration, captions as on-page text, reduced motion and phone layouts. Performance: 3D models and decoders load only when needed. Licensing and honesty: we credit every model and creator, label AI-generated illustrations and AI use, and avoid claiming NASA data or approval we don't have.
